title: Introduce warmup-stabilizer: progressive shape coercion, replay throttler, and eviction safeguards for CUDA-graph replay
author: Anika Patel
description:
Context: we continue to see intermittent warmup flaps where CUDA graph replay is repeatedly invalidated by small, transient shape variations or KV-cache alignment differences. Prior approaches tended to be binary: accept or evict a captured graph. That leads to noisy churn under bursty traffic and observable latency/cold-start regressions.

Summary: this PR implements a "warmup-stabilizer" subcomponent in the CUDA-graph replay path that reduces replay churn by (1) progressively coercing similar-but-not-identical shapes toward a sentinel shape for a bounded number of replays, (2) introducing a replay-throttler state machine that rate-limits aggressive replays per-GPU to avoid contention, and (3) an eviction safeguard that prefers retiring least-recently-probed graphs instead of immediate global invalidation. The net effect is fewer warmup rollbacks, smoother latency distribution during workload shifts, and measurable throughput gains.

Design highlights: Progressive shape coercion: when a replay mismatch is detected, the stabilizer computes a minimal coercion vector that pads/truncates non-batch dims to nearest sentinel bucket (configurable buckets per-model). Coercion is applied only for N=1..3 consecutive replays; coercion levels increase conservatively. If coercion succeeds for the configured window, the graph remains usable and a compatibility score is boosted.

Replay-throttler state machine: per-GPU finite-state machine with states {Idle, Probing, Stabilized, Throttled}. Rapid mismatches move the graph into Throttled state which enforces exponential backoff before the next heavy replay attempt. This prevents runaway kernel contention during hot restarts and allows background priming to complete.

Eviction safeguards: graphs carry probe metadata (last_probe_ts, success_count, compatibility_score). Under memory pressure or when a new capture candidate is required, eviction prefers low-compatibility_score and long-unprobed graphs. We avoid global mass-evictions: only local graphs on the same GPU are evicted unless a sustained fleet-wide incompatibility is observed.

Kernel compatibility scoring: lightweight heuristic that combines kernel-matching fingerprint, coercion distance, and observed latency delta to maintain per-graph scores used by the throttler and eviction policy. Scores are exposed as metrics for debugging.

KV cache alignment: added an alignment tolerance check on replay that will attempt localized KV head-tail alignment corrections before deciding to evict. This was a common root cause in SUP-2321. The alignment correction is cheap (single memcpy of head pointers) and constrained by the same replay window as coercion.

Observability and safety: added metrics (replay_attempts, replay_successes, coercion_applied, throttled_replays, eviction_reasons) and logs at debug/info levels. Feature gated via runtime config flags (default on for canary, off for older customers). New CI tests include unit tests for the state machine, synthetic fuzz harnesses that exercise micro-variations in shape and KV offsets, and an integration canary that replays recorded production traces.

Testing & results: internal canary across two clusters showed a median tail-latency reduction (p95) of ~12ms during scale-up events and a 0.9–1.8% improvement in sustained throughput for chat workloads with fragmented batching. Regression tests added to perf-canary validate that identical-shape capture/replay path remains bit-identical.

Backward compatibility & rollout: no API changes. The stabilizer is opt-in via a config flag per-deployment and can be toggled at runtime. We included a fast rollback hook to disable coercion and immediately evict stabilized graphs.

Why this is different: rather than widening shape guards permissively or adding global heuristics that mask bugs, this change attempts minimal, observable local fixes (coercion + alignment) within a bounded replay window and couples that with throttling and smarter eviction so we avoid oscillations and noisy regressions.

Notes: this PR intentionally does not change kernel selection logic; compatibility_score informs kernel fallback but does not rebind kernels automatically in this change (follow-up change planned).

review_comments: Miguel Santos: overall this looks good, but can you clarify how coercion interacts with quantized kernels? Concerned about subtle numeric effects.

Anika Patel: coercion is shape-only (pad/truncate) and we do not change quantization parameters. We added a unit test that compares post-coercion outputs against a non-coerced baseline for quantized kernels; see runtime/tests/warmup_stabilizer_tests.cc: lines ~120-170.
Priya Desai: the throttler backoff parameters need to be tunable per-deployment. Please surface them via runtime flags and document sane defaults.

Anika Patel: added runtime flags in configs/defaults/runtime_flags.yaml and documented defaults in docs/runtime/warmup-stabilizer.md. Default backoff is exponential with base=1.5 capped at 30s for canary tier.
Ethan Roberts: can we get perf numbers from the canary? I want to ensure there are no regressions for non-fragmented batches.

Anika Patel: attached perf summary in the PR thread and added a perf-canary fixture. Summary: identical-shape throughput flat (+0.1%), fragmented-batch throughput +0.9-1.8%, p95 under scale-up improved ~12ms.

release_notes: Introduce Warmup Stabilizer to reduce CUDA-graph replay churn: progressive shape coercion, replay throttling, KV-cache alignment corrections, and smarter eviction. Opt-in via runtime flag. Improves p95 latency during scale-up and throughput for fragmented batching workloads.
notes: Follow-up tasks: integrate compatibility_score into kernel fallback to allow automatic safe kernel migration (ENG-10014).
Canary rollout: enable for 10% of hosted clusters for two weeks before wider rollout.
Rollback: runtime flag to disable stabilizer and immediate eviction hook included in configs/defaults/runtime_flags.yaml.
